# The Strange Joy of Autumn Walks

I've been thinking about how autumn somehow makes ordinary walks feel significant. Yesterday I wandered without destination, just following the sidewalk wherever it went, and found myself genuinely moved by things I usually ignore.

A single leaf—bright orange, still wet from rain—stuck to the concrete. I actually stopped to look at it. Not because it was rare, but because it seemed to contain something about time passing. Something about the specific moment we're all moving through together.

There's a particular smell right now, too. That mix of wet earth and decomposing leaves that feels less like death and more like transformation. I don't know if that's scientifically accurate, but it's what I feel when I breathe it in.

I passed a house with a porch light on even though it was 4 PM. Someone inside, doing something. Living their afternoon life while the world tilted toward winter. There's something beautiful about that—how everyone is just living, solving small problems, maybe drinking tea, existing in their own small rooms while the seasons turn outside.

I think we underestimate how much our surroundings affect our thinking. A walk in spring might make you ambitious. Summer makes you lazy. But autumn does something stranger—it makes you nostalgic for moments you're still living through. You feel the preciousness of the present tense while you're standing in it.

Maybe that's why I walked so slowly yesterday. Not trying to get anywhere, just trying to stay in that feeling a little longer.
